role: Quick statistics tool for part A: reads threads120.csv, reports rates per kernel and binary.
purpose: The script reads the file `threads120.csv` of one or more part A result folders. For each pair of kernel and binary it prints the number of timed intervals and the lowest, the median and the highest `aggregate_GBps`, which is the rate that the benchmark binary printed for an interval.

main_flow.step: Read the arguments: result folders, `--pool` with optional folders, and `--json`.
Build the list of all folders (each one once) and the list of the folders to pool.

`load` reads `threads120.csv` of each folder. It returns one record per process (one header line) with one entry per interval line: `aggregate_GBps`, the per-thread minimum and maximum, and the pass count.

`rows_of` groups the processes by the pair (kernel, binary). For each group it computes `n`, `min`, `median` and `max` of `aggregate_GBps` over all intervals of the group. It runs once per folder and once more for the pool.
Print the rows as text with `print_text`, or as one JSON list with `--json`.
End with an error message and exit status 1 when a process has a header line and no interval line.

behavior_notes: Rate formula: this script computes no rate. It reads field 7 of an interval line, `aggregate_GBps`, as the benchmark binary printed it (2 decimals). bandwidth.c computes that value as the bytes of all threads, divided by the longest elapsed time of one thread, divided by 1e9 [Ref1]. Each thread measures its own elapsed time. It reads the clock once before its first timed pass and again after each pass over its 256 MiB buffer. The elapsed time runs from the first read to the last read [Ref1]. The old source bandwidth.orig.c does the same [Ref2].

stat_bwx.py, the tool for the csv files of the runner bwx12, uses another formula: the sum over the threads of bytes / own elapsed time / 1e9. No thread has an elapsed time above the longest one. So for one interval that sum cannot be lower than `aggregate_GBps` (before rounding). Part A uses the whole-pass stop, and its threads have different elapsed times. In the 36 `read` intervals of the three part A folders of the rerun the sum is about 1 % to 4 % higher than `aggregate_GBps` (est.: 120 x the column `per_thread_avg_GBps`, which is rounded to 0.01 GB/s) [Ref4].

Lines used: every header line (binary, kernel, round, load, UTC time) and every interval line (field 4, `rep`, is a number). Of an interval line the script reads fields 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9. It does not read field 2 (`threads`), field 6 (`elapsed_s`) or field 10 (`per_thread_avg_GBps`). Lines not used: the `#` comment line, the line of column names and the `best` line of each process.

No interval is left out, and no kernel is treated specially. A part A file also holds processes of the kernels `write`, `copy`, `asmread`, `asmwrite` and `asmcopy` [Ref3]. Each pair of kernel and binary gets its own row.

The old read kernel is the row with kernel `read` and binary `bw_old`. The new read kernel is the row with kernel `read` and binary `bw_new`. The script does not compute the difference between the two rows.
In one part A folder each pair has 2 processes (round 1 and round 2) with 3 intervals each, so `n` is 6 [Ref3]. The statistics do not keep the rounds apart. The lines per process show each round.
The script does not check the thread count, the CPU list or the buffer size. The pattern `HDR` reads these fields of the header line, and `load` does not keep them.

Rounding: `min`, `max` and every interval value are the numbers of the file. `median` is rounded to 3 decimals in the row, and the text report prints it with 2 decimals. The median of an even number of values can have a 5 as its third decimal. The text report formats the binary floating-point number, and it can then print the lower 2-decimal value. Example: the 6 `asmread` intervals of `bw_new` in the first part A folder of the rerun have the median 328.455 GB/s, and the text report prints 328.45. The facts sheet rounds half up. So a median of the facts sheet can differ by 0.01 GB/s from the output of this tool [Ref6].

Role in the final numbers: the facts sheet and the report page use the same rate for part A, the column `aggregate_GBps` [Ref6]. build_facts.py reads the files with the parser of facts_data.py and compares every interval with the output of `load` [Ref5]. The facts sheet records this check as passed for 333 interval lines, among them the 216 interval lines of the three part A folders of the rerun [Ref6].
facts_data.py also uses the pattern `HDR` of this file [Ref5]. Neither build_facts.py nor facts_data.py calls `main`.

words.def: the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means this loop. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.

the four other kernels of bw_old and bw_new. `write` fills a buffer. `copy` copies one buffer to a second buffer. `asmwrite` and `asmcopy` are hand-written loops for the same two jobs. They are not read kernels.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.

a process is one start of a benchmark binary. An interval is one timed measurement inside a process. bwx12 times a sequence of kernels and repeats the sequence: each repeat is a round (counted from 0), and the position is the place of a kernel in the sequence (counted from 0). In part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
the read test of 2026-11-17 with 120 threads, run after the memory speed was lowered to 7200 MT/s (million transfers per second). Part A is one of its parts.
1 GB is 1e9 bytes. Every rate is in GB/s.
the result file of part A. For each benchmark process, ra.sh appends one header line and then the output of the process.
the script that runs part A. It starts one process per binary and kernel, in two rounds.

a line that starts with `-- binary`. ra.sh writes it directly before it starts a process. It names the binary, the kernel, the thread count, the CPU list, the buffer size, the round, the load and the UTC time.

a csv line that the benchmark binary prints for one timed interval. Its 10 fields are: kernel, threads, bytes_per_thread, rep, total_bytes, elapsed_s, aggregate_GBps, per_thread_min_GBps, per_thread_max_GBps, per_thread_avg_GBps. The field elapsed_s holds the longest elapsed time of one thread [Ref1].
field 7 of an interval line: the bytes of all threads, divided by the longest elapsed time of one thread, divided by 1e9.

fields 8, 9 and 10 of an interval line. Fields 8 and 9 are the lowest and the highest rate of one thread in the interval. Field 10 is the mean of the rates of all threads. The rate of a thread is its bytes divided by its own elapsed time, divided by 1e9 [Ref1].

`total_bytes` divided by `bytes_per_thread` of an interval line, rounded down. For the kernels `read`, `write`, `asmread` and `asmwrite` this is the number of buffer passes that all 120 threads together completed in the interval [Ref1]. For `copy` and `asmcopy` the binary counts read plus written bytes, as the `#` comment line of each process says. So the same division gives 2 x the number of buffer passes for these two kernels.

the 1-minute load average of Linux (the average number of tasks that are runnable or wait for disk input and output). ra.sh reads it directly before it starts a process and writes it into the header line.
the stop rule of bandwidth.c: after the minimum time (0.5 s here) each thread finishes the pass over its buffer that it is in. The threads stop at different times.
the intervals of several folders taken together as one group.
the middle value of a sorted list. For an even number of values Python takes the mean of the two middle values.
the facts sheet is the file FACTS.md with its data file facts.json. It is the detailed record of the rerun. build_facts.py writes both from the raw result files and uses the parsers of facts_data.py.
the file `whole-chip-rerun-7200.html`. The script make_report.py writes it from facts.json.
estimated, not measured directly.

functions.name: load
functions.what: Reads `threads120.csv` of a folder. Returns one record per process with `aggregate_GBps`, per-thread minimum and maximum, and pass count of every interval.

functions.name: rows_of
functions.what: Groups processes by (kernel, binary). Computes n, min, median and max of `aggregate_GBps` over all intervals of each group.

functions.name: print_text
functions.what: Prints one group as text: a statistics line per kernel and binary, then one line per process with every interval.

functions.name: main
functions.what: Parses the arguments, loads every folder, builds the rows per folder and for the pool, prints text or JSON.
